title: Angles: Naming, Estimating and Measuring with a Protractor
seo_title: Grade 6 Angles Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Recognise, describe, classify, estimate and measure angles in degrees using a protractor: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex and revolution.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 6 angles worksheets: naming angles, estimating, measuring with a protractor and reflex angles. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Centre on the vertex, 0° on one arm.
key_sub: Estimate first, then read the right scale.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Acute: less than 90°. Right: 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°. Revolution: 360°.
  • To measure, put the centre of the protractor on the vertex and the 0° line on one arm.
  • Read the scale that starts at 0° on that arm.
  • Estimate first, so you choose the right scale.

Examples

Example

An angle a bit bigger than a right angle

obtuse

about 100°

Answer: the protractor shows 105°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
The wrong scaleStart from 0° on one arm.
Arm lengthLong arms do not make a big angle.
Obtuse or reflex?Reflex is more than 180°.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 6 say about angles?
faq.a: Recognise, describe, classify and measure angles, including acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex and revolution, using a protractor.

faq.q: How do I measure a reflex angle?
faq.a: Measure the small angle and take it away from 360°.

items.q: Classify the marked angle.
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 35°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 125°.

items.q: Classify the marked angle.
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a quarter turn. The small square shows it. Turning the angle does not change its size or its name.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 160°.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes around the outside. This angle is 230°. (The gap between the arms is 130°, but the arc marks the big angle around the outside.)

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is less than half a right angle (45°). About 30° fits. (150° is what the other scale of a protractor would say.)

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is about half of a right angle, so it is about 45°.

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle looks like a square corner, so it is about 90°. (It is 88°.)
The angle is a bit more than a right angle (90°), but less than 135°. About 120° fits. (60° would be acute.)
The angle is about halfway between a right angle (90°) and a straight angle (180°), so it is about 135°.
The arms almost make a straight line (180°), so the angle is about 170°. (10° is the small gap left to make a straight line, and 190° would be reflex.)
The arc goes around the outside and is a little more than a straight angle (180°), so it is about 200°. (160° is the gap between the arms, the angle on the other side.)
The arc goes around the outside and leaves a gap of about a right angle. 360° − 90° = 270°. (90° is the gap, not the marked angle.)
The gap between the arms is about 45°, half a right angle. The marked angle goes around the outside: 360° − 45° = 315°. (45° is only the gap.)
The marked angle is more than a straight angle (180°) but less than three right angles (270°). Halfway between is 225°. (135° is the gap on the other side: 360° − 225° = 135°.)

items.q: Which angle is closest to 45°?
items.e: 45° is half a right angle. B is about half of a square corner. A is nearly a right angle, C is very small and D is obtuse.
270° is three right angles, so the gap between the arms is a right angle. C leaves a square-corner gap. A is about 200°, B is about 300° and D is about 330°.
The size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms, not the length of the arms. A opens the widest (about 150°), even though its arms are the shortest.

items.q: An angle is a little smaller than a right angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. A little smaller than 90° is about 80°. 100° is a little bigger.

items.q: An angle is a little bigger than a straight angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A straight angle is 180°. A little bigger is about 190°, a reflex angle. 170° is a little smaller.

items.q: Which angle is closer to a straight angle: 165° or 200°?
What angle is halfway between a right angle and a straight angle?
items.e: Halfway between 90° and 180° is 135°, because 90° + 45° = 135°. (270° comes from adding 90° + 180°.)

items.q: How many degrees are in three quarters of a full turn?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. One quarter is 90°, so three quarters is 3 × 90° = 270°. (75° comes from mixing up three quarters with 75%.)

items.q: An angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than three right angles. Which could it be?
items.e: It must be between 180° and 270°. Only 230° fits. 130° and 170° are less than 180°, and 290° is more than 270°.

items.q: Tumi estimates an angle as about 135°. Then she measures it with a protractor and reads 45°. What should she do?
items.e: 45° is far from the estimate of 135°, so Tumi probably read the wrong scale. The other scale gives 180° − 45° = 135°, which matches the estimate.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts anti-clockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 40. The outer scale says 140 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 20 and the other is at 95. The angle is the difference: 95° − 20° = 75°.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 40 and the other is at 150. The angle is the difference: 150° − 40° = 110°.

items.q: Where do you put the centre of the protractor when you measure an angle?
c: in the middle of an arm
at the end of an arm
items.e: The centre goes on the vertex, where the two arms meet. Then line up one arm with 0.

items.q: One arm of an angle is on 0 of the outer scale. Which scale should you read?
c: the scale with the smaller number
the scale with the bigger number
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Dumisani measures an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle. The arm crosses the protractor at 35 and 145. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle smaller than a right angle is acute, less than 90°, so it is 35°. 145 is on the other scale.

items.q: Chloe measures an angle and writes 40°. The angle is clearly obtuse. What should she have written?
items.e: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Chloe read the wrong scale: the other scale gives 180° − 40° = 140°.

items.q: Musa wanted to construct an angle of 50°. His base arm is on 0 of the inner scale. The picture shows what he drew. What angle did he actually draw?
items.e: Read the inner scale, because the base arm is on its 0: the second arm is at 130, so the angle is 130°. Musa used 50 on the outer scale by mistake. 180° − 50° = 130°.

items.q: Vusi wanted to construct an angle of 70°. His base arm is on 0 of the outer scale. The picture shows what he drew. What angle did he actually draw?
items.e: The base arm is on 0 of the outer scale, so read the outer scale: the second arm is at 110, so the angle is 110°. Vusi used 70 on the inner scale by mistake. 180° − 70° = 110°.
The two angles go all the way around the vertex, so they add up to 360°. 360° − 70° = 290°. (110° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The two angles go all the way around the vertex, so they add up to 360°. 360° − 125° = 235°. (55° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The two angles go all the way around the vertex, so they add up to 360°. 360° − 40° = 320°. (140° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The two angles go all the way around the vertex, so they add up to 360°. 360° − 155° = 205°. (25° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The two angles add up to 360°. 360° − 250° = 110°. (70° comes from 250° − 180°, and 610° from adding.)
The two angles add up to 360°. 360° − 300° = 60°. (120° comes from 300° − 180°, and 660° from adding.)

items.q: The protractor measures the angle between the two arms. What is the reflex angle between the same arms?
items.e: On the inner scale the angle is 75°. The reflex angle goes the other way around. Together they make a full turn: 360° − 75° = 285°. (105° is the reading on the wrong scale.)

items.q: The protractor measures the angle between the two arms. What is the reflex angle between the same arms?
items.e: The left arm is on 0 of the outer scale, so the angle is 50°. The reflex angle is 360° − 50° = 310°. (230° comes from reading 130 on the wrong scale: 360° − 130° = 230°.)

items.q: To find a reflex angle, Lerato measures the angle on the other side. It is 130°. What is the reflex angle?
items.e: The two angles go all the way around the vertex, so they make a full turn: 360°. 360° − 130° = 230°. (50° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)

items.q: The gap between the arms of a reflex angle is 45°. How big is the reflex angle?

items.e: The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 70° = 290°. (110° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 100° = 260°. (80° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 145° = 215°. (35° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 35° = 325°. (145° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)
The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 230° = 130°.
The clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same two arms add up to a full turn, 360°. 360° − 270° = 90°.

items.q: The arrow shows a turn from one arm to the other. Which describes the turn?
items.e: The arrow turns the same way as the hands of a clock, so it is clockwise. It turns less than a right angle: about 60°. The anti-clockwise angle between the same arms would be about 300°.
The arrow turns the opposite way to the hands of a clock, so it is anti-clockwise. It goes past a straight angle, so it is reflex: about 250°. The clockwise angle between the same arms is about 110°.

items.q: The clockwise angle and the anti-clockwise angle between the same two arms always add up to …
items.e: Turning one way and then the other way between the same two arms makes one full turn: 360°.

items.q: The anti-clockwise angle between two arms is 80°. Liam says the clockwise angle is 100°, because they add up to 180°. Is he right?
items.e: Clockwise and anti-clockwise angles between the same arms add up to 360°, not 180°. 360° − 80° = 280°.

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 4 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 spaces between the numbers go around a full turn, 360°, so each space is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. At 4 o’clock the hands are 4 spaces apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 10 o’clock?
items.e: From 10 to 12 is 2 hour spaces. Each space is 30°, so 2 × 30° = 60°. (300° is the reflex angle the other way around.)

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?
items.e: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so 6° each minute. 20 × 6° = 120°. (240° is the other 40 minutes.)

items.q: A classroom door is opened so that it makes an angle of 100° with the wall. How do you classify this angle?
items.e: 100° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

items.q: In a circle graph of favourite sports, the section for soccer makes an angle of 120° at the centre. What fraction of the circle is it?
items.e: 120° out of 360°: 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so it is one third. (One half would be 180°, and one quarter 90°.)

items.q: A wind turbine has 3 blades spaced equally around the centre. What is the angle between two blades next to each other?
items.e: The 3 equal angles go all the way around: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. (60° comes from 180° ÷ 3.)

items.q: A cedar tree leans after a storm. It makes an angle of 80° with the flat ground on one side. What angle does it make with the ground on the other side?
items.e: The flat ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°. 180° − 80° = 100°. (10° comes from 90° − 80°.)

items.q: A Ferris wheel has 10 cars spaced equally around its centre. What angle at the centre is between two cars next to each other?
items.e: The 10 equal angles go all the way around: 360° ÷ 10 = 36°. (18° comes from 180° ÷ 10.)

items.q: In coding class, Sibusiso’s robot faces north and turns 90° clockwise three times. What single anti-clockwise turn would get it to the same direction?
items.e: 3 × 90° = 270° clockwise. A clockwise turn and a anti-clockwise turn that end in the same place add up to 360°: 360° − 270° = 90° anti-clockwise.

items.q: Tshepo hikes a trail in Stanley Park. At a bend, the angle between the two straight parts of the trail is 150°. How many degrees did he turn at the bend?
items.e: Walking straight on would be 180°. The trail bends to 150°, so Tshepo turned 180° − 150° = 30°. (150° is the angle between the paths, not the turn.)

items.q: What is the reflex angle between the hands of a clock at 2 o’clock?
items.e: The smaller angle is 2 × 30° = 60°. The reflex angle goes the other way around: 360° − 60° = 300°.

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn from 3:00 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.?
items.e: 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour, so three quarter turns: 3 × 90° = 270°, a reflex angle.

items.q: On pizza day, a round pizza is cut into 8 equal slices from the centre. Refilwe eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the slices that are left make?
items.e: Each slice is 360° ÷ 8 = 45°. 5 slices are left: 5 × 45° = 225°, a reflex angle. (135° is the 3 slices that were eaten.)

items.q: A classroom door is opened so that it makes an angle of 100° with the wall. What is the name of this angle?
items.e: 100° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

items.q: Naledi is canoeing at the cottage, facing west. She turns the canoe 90° anti-clockwise. Which way is she facing now?
items.e: Anti-clockwise from west goes to south (north → west → south → east). North would be 90° clockwise.

items.q: In a circle graph, the section for “soccer” makes an angle of 120° at the centre. What fraction of the circle is it?
items.e: 120° out of 360°: 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so it is one third. (One half would be 180°, and one quarter 90°.)

items.q: A lawn sprinkler waters while it turns 150° anti-clockwise. What angle around the sprinkler does it not water?
items.e: The watered angle and the dry angle make a full turn: 360° − 150° = 210°. (30° comes from 180° − 150°.)

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn from 7:15 a.m. to 7:45 a.m.?
items.e: 30 minutes is half an hour, so half a turn: 360° ÷ 2 = 180°, a straight angle.

items.q: In coding class, Ayanda’s robot faces north and turns 90° clockwise three times. What anti-clockwise turn would get it to the same direction?
items.e: 3 × 90° = 270° clockwise. Clockwise and anti-clockwise turns that end in the same place add up to 360°: 360° − 270° = 90° anti-clockwise.

items.q: Pieter writes code for a sprite that turns left (anti-clockwise) 60°. What right (clockwise) turn would end in the same direction?
items.e: The two turns add up to 360°: 360° − 60° = 300° clockwise. (120° comes from 180° − 60°.)
